title: How Much Does a Commercial HVAC System Cost?
h1: How Much Does a Commercial HVAC System Cost?
description: Commercial HVAC cost depends on building size, system type, roof and electrical work, permits and how the space is used. Here's what shapes the number.
quick_answer: Commercial HVAC cost varies widely because no two buildings are alike. The biggest factors are the type of system, such as rooftop units, split systems or VRF, plus the total capacity needed, how the space is used, roof and electrical work, ductwork, controls and permits. An on-site evaluation and load calculation are the only reliable way to get a real number.
body:
What types of commercial HVAC systems are there?

The system type sets the starting point for cost, installation time and maintenance needs.

  • Packaged rooftop units (RTUs): heating and cooling in one cabinet on the roof, connected to ducts below. Common on retail, office and light industrial buildings.
  • Split systems: an outdoor condenser paired with an indoor air handler or furnace. Often used in smaller offices, medical suites and restaurants.
  • Ductless and VRF systems: one or more outdoor units serving many indoor units, each zone controlled separately. Good for buildings with varied spaces or no room for ducts.
  • Larger central systems: chillers, boilers and air handlers for big buildings. These are much more involved projects.

What affects the cost of a commercial HVAC system?

  • Size and capacity: measured in tons of cooling. Square footage matters, but so do ceiling height, windows, insulation and occupancy.
  • How the space is used: a restaurant kitchen, server room, salon or medical office has very different heating, cooling and ventilation needs than a warehouse.
  • Ventilation requirements: commercial spaces must bring in a certain amount of outside air under code, which affects equipment size.
  • Roof work: crane lifts, new curbs, roof penetrations and structural checks for rooftop equipment.
  • Electrical: new circuits, disconnects or service upgrades.
  • Ductwork: reusing existing ducts is cheaper than redesigning them for a new layout.
  • Controls: basic thermostats versus networked controls or a building management system.
  • Permits, plans and inspections: commercial projects often require engineered plans and more inspection steps than residential work.
  • Timing and access: after-hours work to avoid disrupting a business, or tight access in older buildings, adds labor.

Is it a replacement or new construction?

Replacing an existing rooftop unit with a similar one on the same curb is the most straightforward project. Changing the size, adding zones, converting a tenant space for a new use, or building out a new space involves design work, permits and more labor.

Tenant improvements are common in San Diego and Orange County, where office and retail suites change hands and layouts often. A space that used to be offices may need very different airflow as a restaurant or fitness studio.

Does building location matter?

It can. Buildings near the coast deal with salt air that corrodes outdoor coils and cabinets, so coated coils and more frequent rinsing may be worth considering. Inland buildings face hotter summers and more cooling load. Dust from Santa Ana winds and wildfire smoke can clog filters and coils quickly in both. These conditions affect equipment choice, filter selection and how often the system needs service.

What ongoing costs should you plan for?

The install price is only part of what a system costs over its life. Budget for:

  • Energy use: often the largest long-term cost. Higher-efficiency equipment and good controls reduce it.
  • Preventive maintenance: regular filter changes, coil cleaning, belt checks and inspections. Many businesses schedule quarterly or seasonal visits.
  • Repairs: older equipment and units exposed to salt air near the coast tend to need more attention.
  • Duct and exhaust cleaning: dusty ducts and commercial dryer vents in laundromats, gyms and multi-unit buildings need periodic cleaning.

How do you get an accurate commercial HVAC price?

  1. Have a technician evaluate the building, existing equipment, roof and electrical service.
  2. Get a load calculation that reflects how the space is actually used.
  3. Compare equipment options side by side, including efficiency and maintenance needs.
  4. Ask what's included: permits, crane, roof work, controls, startup and testing.
  5. Plan the schedule around business hours so the install doesn't shut you down longer than necessary.

Repair or replace?

If a unit is older, needs repeated repairs or can't keep the space comfortable on hot days, replacement often makes more sense than continuing to fix it. Our commercial HVAC team works with offices, retail, restaurants, property managers and multi-unit buildings across San Diego and Orange County, and can evaluate your building and give you a free estimate.
faqs: How long does a commercial HVAC system last?
It depends on the equipment, how hard it runs, maintenance and exposure to salt air or heat. Regular preventive maintenance is the biggest factor you control.
How often should commercial HVAC be serviced?
Many businesses schedule maintenance quarterly or at least twice a year, before cooling and heating seasons. Busy spaces like restaurants and gyms may need more frequent filter changes.
Can you replace a rooftop unit without closing my business?
Often, yes. Many replacements can be scheduled early in the morning, after hours or on weekends to limit disruption.
Do commercial HVAC projects need permits?
Yes. Most commercial installs and replacements need permits, and larger projects may require engineered plans and multiple inspections.
